property_summary: For every interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) whenever interfaceId equals IAccessControl's id OR equals IERC165's id (i.e., supportsInterface should be true for either interface); the mutant (which uses &&) will incorrectly return false for interfaceId equal to IAccessControl.interfaceId (or IERC165) unless both ids match simultaneously, so the mutant fails for such inputs.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true if interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId OR type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant requiring both (AND) will return false for at least one of those interface ids and thus violate this rule.

For every bytes4 x, C.supportsInterface(x) returns true whenever x equals IAccessControl's id or IERC165's id; the mutant changed the OR to AND, so it will return false for those individual ids and thus violate this rule for some inputs.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true if interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant changed the OR to AND, so it will return false for those individual interface ids and thus violate this rule for some inputs.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true if interfaceId equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId OR type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant changed the OR to AND so it will return false for at least one of those interface ids, violating this rule.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the correct contract returns true exactly when interfaceId == IAccessControl or when its super.supportsInterface reports true; the mutant inverts the equality and thus will return true for any interfaceId that is NOT IAccessControl (breaking the rule for many inputs).

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference C returns true iff (interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) || super.supportsInterface(interfaceId); the mutant inverts the equality and thus will return true for most interfaceIds that are NOT IAccessControl, violating the equivalence for some inputs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the correct contract returns supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId || super.supportsInterface(interfaceId)); the mutant inverts the equality with IAccessControl and therefore will disagree for many interfaceIds (notably those not equal to IAccessControl).

For every 4-byte interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns (interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) || super.supportsInterface(interfaceId); the mutant inverts the equality with IAccessControl and thus will return a different boolean for some interfaceIds (those not equal to IAccessControl).

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference C always returns true exactly when interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or when super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true; the mutant inverts the equality check with IAccessControl and thus will return a different boolean for some interfaceIds (notably those not equal to IAccessControl).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct contract's supportsInterface may return true for some ids (specifically it returns true for IERC165 and IAccessControl interface IDs when queried), while the mutant always returns false; the test asserts that calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) does not always return false by checking that at least one known interface id (fuzzed) returns true for the correct contract (so the mutant will fail for that input).

For any bytes4 interfaceId input, the reference contract's supportsInterface will return true for at least one interface id value in the domain (specifically when the id equals type(IERC165).interfaceId) whereas the mutant always returns false, so there exists an input (the IERC165 id) where the results differ.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, calling supportsInterface on the correct contract never reverts and for the specific interface id equal to type(IERC165).interfaceId it returns true; the mutant always returns false causing a mismatch for that input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract C never reverts and returns true for at least the IERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) when that exact bytes4 is supplied; the mutant always returns false so for that interface id the returned value differs — thus there exists an input (the IERC165 id) where the mutant breaks the rule.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C never reverts on supportsInterface and, when queried with the interface id equal to type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (passed as a fuzz parameter), returns true; the mutant that always returns false will return false for that input, so there exists an input where the return differs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the correct contract returns true iff the id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (as implemented via super check), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns true for all ids — so there exist ids where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract only reports support for interfaces it actually implements (IERC165 and IAccessControl via super), whereas the mutant incorrectly reports support for all interfaceIds (always returns true), so there exist interfaceIds for which reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface call never returns true for arbitrary ids that are not IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. it only returns true for the interfaces it implements), whereas the mutant returns true for all ids, so there exist fuzzed interfaceId values where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the correct contract's supportsInterface never returns true for arbitrary ids that are not supported by IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. it only returns true for interfaces it actually implements via super.supportsInterface), whereas the mutant returns true for all ids — therefore there exist fuzzed interfaceId values for which the reference returns false but the mutant returns true.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface call never returns true for ids it doesn't implement (it only returns true when super supports it), whereas the mutant always returns true — therefore there exist interfaceId values where reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true for IERC165's interfaceId (0x01ffc9a7) and also returns true for IAccessControl's interfaceId (type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) when queried, while the mutant that defers only to super may fail to report support for IAccessControl for some interfaceId (specifically IAccessControl's id).

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C returns true for IERC165's interfaceId (0x01ffc9a7) and specifically returns true for IAccessControl's interface id when queried (because it explicitly checks IAccessControl), while the mutant that defers entirely to super can return false for the IAccessControl id — so the property: calling supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) completes and returns true for the reference but may return false for the mutant.

For every bytes4 id, calling supportsInterface(id) does not revert; in particular, the correct contract always reports support for IERC165 (0x01ffc9a7) while the buggy variant that removed the explicit IAccessControl check can differ on IAccessControl's id — so the reference always returns true for IERC165's interface id and the mutant can return false for IAccessControl's id (the test fuzzes the interface id to find the mismatch).

For every bytes4 interface id, the reference C reports support for IERC165.interfaceId (0x01ffc9a7) and in particular always returns true for IERC165; the mutant that delegates only to super may still return true for IERC165 but will return false for IAccessControl.interfaceId, so the general rule is: calling supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) always completes and returns true on the reference, while the mutant can return false for at least some interface ids (notably IAccessControl), which the fuzzer can find by supplying interface ids — we assert that supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) is true (reference satisfies for all inputs) and the mutant fails for some inputs by differing on IAccessControl id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, the reference C always returns true for IERC165.interfaceId when called via supportsInterface (it supports ERC165) while the mutant that removes the explicit IAccessControl check can still return a different boolean for other interface ids (notably IAccessControl); we assert that supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) returns true on the reference for all inputs, a property the mutant can violate for some interface ids it reports differently.

For every role and account, the reference always returns true iff the account is stored as a member for that role; the mutant negates membership so there exist role/account pairs where hasRole returns the opposite (i.e. reference true but mutant false, or vice versa).
